original_question: Should numerical work on Painleve equations use integrable discretizations, namely discrete Painleve equations that tend to the associated continuous Painleve equations in an appropriate continuum limit, instead of relying only on generic discretizations of the differential equations?
target_in_paper: Section 4, Open Problem 4.1, third bullet: the paper asks whether numerical study of the continuous Painlevé equations should use an "integrable discretization," i.e. a discrete Painlevé equation that limits to the corresponding continuous Painlevé equation in an appropriate continuum limit. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2019/006/sigma19-006.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right target almost verbatim: it is about numerical work on Painlevé equations, about using discrete Painlevé equations as integrable discretizations, and about the required continuum-limit relation to the associated continuous Painlevé equation. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2019/006/sigma19-006.pdf))
missing_details: The paper frames this as an open methodological question in the development of numerical software for studying Painlevé equations, not as a settled recommendation. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2019/006/sigma19-006.pdf))

The immediate comparison class in context is standard generic ODE methods such as Runge–Kutta; your draft gestures at this, but the paper introduces it explicitly just before Open Problem 4.1. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2019/006/sigma19-006.pdf))

The scope is the continuous Painlevé equations as objects of numerical study; discrete Painlevé equations enter only as candidate integrable discretizations of those continuous equations. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2019/006/sigma19-006.pdf))

The surrounding Section 4 context says the broader numerical agenda is to exploit the integrable/global structure of Painlevé equations, including isomonodromy and the associated Riemann–Hilbert problem; this is part of the intended scope even though your draft isolates only the discretization bullet. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2019/006/sigma19-006.pdf))

The paper does not specify a particular member of PI–PVI, a particular discrete Painlevé scheme, a step-size regime, or a formal convergence/error criterion; the question is intentionally posed at this higher methodological level. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2019/006/sigma19-006.pdf))

There are no ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, operator, nilpotency, or "for all sufficiently large m" hypotheses here; those kinds of algebraic conditions are not part of this paper's formulation of the problem. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2019/006/sigma19-006.pdf))

Your phrase "instead of relying only on generic discretizations" is slightly stronger than the paper, which asks whether one should use an integrable discretization, without formally stating an exclusive replacement of all generic discretizations. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2019/006/sigma19-006.pdf))
refined_question: When developing numerical software for the continuous Painlevé equations, should one use an "integrable discretization"—that is, a discrete Painlevé equation which is itself integrable and which tends to the corresponding continuous Painlevé equation in an appropriate continuum limit—rather than relying only on generic ODE discretizations such as standard Runge–Kutta-type methods? ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2019/006/sigma19-006.pdf))
justification: This is the nearest official formulation of your draft in the paper: the third bullet of Open Problem 4.1 asks whether one should use an "integrable discretization" of the Painlevé equations, immediately after noting that discrete Painlevé equations are integrable discrete equations with the appropriate continuum limit. The surrounding Section 4 discussion shows that the author's concern is numerical software for Painlevé equations and that the broader methodological backdrop is to exploit integrability, including Riemann–Hilbert/isomonodromy information, rather than treating the equations only as generic nonlinear ODEs. The shorter list of open problems in the introduction confirms that the paper's numerical open problem is precisely about software that uses the integrable structure of Painlevé equations. ([sigma-journal.com](https://sigma-journal.com/2019/006/sigma19-006.pdf))
